rows_detail.query: will re-indexing repair a chunker bug
rows_detail.answer: No, fixing a chunker-selection bug does not repair an affected corpus by re-running `recall index`; the run reports "N unchanged" and leaves every wrongly-split chunk exactly where it was.

rows_detail.query: what happens to a project's memory when I rename its directory
rows_detail.answer: Renaming a project directory causes its memory store to be keyed on the project path, so a fresh, empty store appears under the new slug while the old one keeps every memo and becomes invisible—no error, no warning, and the index loaded each session is simply the new empty one. To avoid this, before renaming, move `~/.claude/projects/<old-slug>/memory/` into the new slug at rename time, since there is no later signal that anything is missing. If a memory store looks thin for a project with history, list `~/.claude/projects/` and look for a slug matching an old name of the directory; two stores for one project is the tell. The same key derivation strands stores when a user profile changes, and archived (not deleted) stores are kept at `~/.claude/archive/stranded-memory-stores-2026-08-15/` with a README recording what was recovered and what was deliberately left unmerged.

rows_detail.query: what happens if I mix two embedding models in one tenant
rows_detail.answer: Mixing two embedding models in one tenant leads to silently wrong retrieval. The system can detect dimension mismatches (pgvector rejects different-width embeddings), but when models have the same dimension (e.g., voyage-4 and voyage-code-3 are both 1024), the SQL succeeds, cosine comparisons are computed between vectors from different models, and the ranking becomes garbage that looks exactly like a valid ranking, with no error or warning.

rows_detail.query: why did writing a file with python change every line ending
rows_detail.answer: On Windows, Python's `Path.write_text(...)` in default text mode translates `\n` to `\r\n`, converting the whole file from LF to CRLF. This happens even when the repository is configured for LF endings via `.gitattributes`, so `git status` shows the file as modified with no content difference, and `git ls-files --eol` shows `i/lf w/crlf` (index LF, working tree CRLF).

rows_detail.answer: No, refusing known-bad values is not enough. It is a negative check that closes only the failure modes you thought of, and everything the producer never emits—or that predates the field—walks straight through.

rows_detail.answer: When a gate closes early, its paired scheduled deadman check must be cancelled or repointed in the same session, and when the scheduled gate task fires, the issue state must be read first — if state is CLOSED, the correct output is a SUPERSEDED note on the issue, not a run.

rows_detail.query: what is wrong with a guard I wrote that always passes
rows_detail.answer: A guard that always passes produces a "false green" — it never fails, so it looks like protection but tests nothing. It is dangerous because it creates an asymmetry: a guard that cannot fail gives a false sense of security (false green), while a guard that cannot pass discards good work (false red). The sharper version is that a guard that "reads as protection and cannot fire" has a twin: a guard that cannot pass. Both look like rigour but test nothing. The question to catch the first is "what would make this fire?" and for the second "what would make this pass?".
